INTEREST OF THE AMICI CURIAE
Amici are experts in health care practice, health
care law, and bioethics . 1  Amici bring expertise in
health care, which integrates mental health care as
an essential component, and which is often carried out
purely through speech. Amici also have expertise in
health care regulation, through which the state has
maintained standards of clinical practice—even when
such practice is carried out through speech. A list of
amici is appended to this brief.
SUMMARY OF ARGUMENT
Since the beginning of modern medical practice, 2
states have regulated standards of clinical care —
including care concerning mental health and care
delivered through speech. Such regulation has taken
many forms. Tort law has enforced prevailing
standards of care, even when the care was delivered
solely through speech. Licensing and other regulatory
regimes have disciplined unlicensed individuals
holding themselves out as professionals, who often

1 No counsel for a party authored this brief in whole or part, and
no party other than amici or their counsel made a monetary contribution to the preparation or submission of the brief. See Supreme Court Rule 37.6.
2 Medical historians date the birth of modern medical practice
to the late nineteenth century, when empirical methods and
germ theory were developed and incorporated into clinical care.
Until then, medical practice relied on many approaches, including the belief that “illness … was … caused by an imbalance of
the four humors” and ameliorated through techniques such as
“bleeding” using leeches, among other approaches. Paul Starr,
The Social Transformation of American Medicine  38, 95 (Basic
Books 1982). See Br. of Medical History Scholars and Historians
as Amici Curiae in Support of Respondents 13-17 [hereinafter
Historians’ Br.].

2


offered dubious scientific theories, as well as licensed
professionals who engaged in clinical speech that was
inaccurate or deviated from then -prevailing
standards of care. And governments have created and
standardized the very vocabulary of health  care—
diagnostic codes, procedur al codes, and data
standards—without which clinical communication
would be impossible. These frameworks apply equally
to mental health  care. And for more than a century,
such regulation of clinical communication has never
been unde rstood to infringe the First Amendment,
because it governs the delivery of health  care, not
speech as speech.
These regulatory efforts reflect the realities of
clinical practice. In the pre -antibiotic era, when
effective procedures were scarce, physicians primarily
advised patients through speech: how to prevent
illness through hygiene; when to let an ailment run
its course; how to prepare for death. Despite scientific
advances, that remains true today. Pediatricians,
primary care physicians, and mental health
professionals then —and now —spend much of their
practice counseling patients and families in
encounters tha t consist only of speech. Licensing
standards have long helped consolidate clinical
practice into a discernible profession, and
standardized vocabularies ensure that those
standards are applied consistently.
State courts and legislatures have long recognized
mental health as critical to the delivery of health care.
Modern statutes confirm this parity: the Affordable
Care Act treats mental health services as “essential
health benefits,” Health Insurance Portability and
Accountability Act of 1996 (HIPAA) applies stringent

3


protections to psychotherapy notes, and state mental
health licensing boards regulate counseling under
frameworks parallel to those that govern medicine.
For example, in Colorado, while licensed professional
counselors may not “engage in the practice of
medicine,” 3  they are nevertheless subject to
comprehensive state oversight, including licensure,
discipline, and scope -of-practice rules that regulate
their clinical speech in the same way that medical
boards regulate physicians. This reflects clinical
reality: mental health directly affects physical health,
and biological factors strongly influence mental
health.
The regulation of clinical practice, including care
delivered primarily or exclusively through speech,
relies heavily on professional expertise. Malpractice
standards are defined in part by professional custom
and the testimony of experts regarding the sta ndard
of care. Licensing boards rely on their licensees’
expertise when imposing disciplinary sanctions. And
regulatory agencies incorporate evidence -based
guidelines developed by professional associations.
This ensures that clinical practice of all kinds is held
to the same standards, whether carried out through
conduct, speech, or both.
These regulatory efforts are distinct from other
speech regimes that do not set standards of care and
may apply even outside clinical practice. See Nat’l
Inst. of Fam. & Life Advocs. v. Becerra, 585 U.S. 755,
756 (2018) (where speech regime did not pertain to
clinical standard of care) [hereinafter NIFLA]. For
example, privacy laws restrict disclosure of a patient’s

3 Colo. Rev. Stat. § 12-245-210(1).

4


visit whether or not clinical care is rendered. Such
situations present different First Amendment
questions and standards that do not apply to this case.
The Colorado law at issue here plainly regulates
clinical care  by prohibiting a form of counseling
treatment deemed harmful by every major
professional association: medical sexual orientation
and gender identity change efforts. Applying strict
scrutiny to such a law under the First Amendment
would displace professional judgment, de stabilize
longstanding regulatory traditions, and force courts
around the nation into the business of defining clinical
care standards. The Constitution does not compel that
result.
ARGUMENT
I. MENTAL HEALTH CARE IS AN INTEGRAL
PART OF CLINICAL CARE
Although Petitioner seeks to divorce the regulation
of “healthcare professions as a whole” from that of
mental health  care, Pet ’r’s Br. at 43,  both clinically
and legally, psychological treatment is inseparable
from the broader practice of clinical care. Traditional
approaches to health  care regulation more generally
should guide the Court.
A. Science confirms that mental health is
integral to overall health
Mental health care —including psychology and
counseling services—is not distinct from clinical care
but is part of its core. Chronic stress contributes to
cardiovascular disease, immune dysfunction,
hypertension, digestive problems, ulcers, and genetic

5

damage. 4  Mental illness itself often has biological
origins, including genetic and neurobiological bases.5
In recent decades, psychological interventions,
such as cognitive behavioral therapy, problem-solving
therapy, and interpersonal therapy, have been
validated through randomized clinical trials and
meta-analyses. 6  These treatments address
depression, anxiety, post -traumatic stress disorder,
obsessive-compulsive disorder, and eating disorders ,
among other conditions .7 Data from routine practice
settings have yielded similar treatment outcomes.8
Given the demonstrated effectiveness of many
psychological interventions, prominent professional
medical associations, including the American
Academies of Pediatrics and Family Physicians, and
the American College of Physicians recommend
psychological treatment , including in clinical

frequently screen and treat patients for mental health

B. Legal frameworks treat mental health
care as part of the broader practice of
health care delivery
Mental health care and its providers are regulated
by state and federal law as part of the broader
framework of health care regulation. For example, the
Privacy Rule, which implements HIPAA, applies with
equal force to practitioners who provide mental health
services as practitioners who address physical health
needs.13 In fact, the Privacy Rule imposes heightened
protections for psychotherapy notes.14 The Affordable
Care Act classifies mental health  care among its
Essential Health Benefits (EHBs). 15  Mental health -
related diagnostic codes are fully integrated into the
standardized diagnostic code set  maintained by the
federal government, see infra Section II.B.3. 16  And
oversight of the licensed practice of mental health care
(e.g., psychology or professional counseling) is usually
performed by divisions of the  same state agencies
responsible for general health  care oversight or
professional licensing , using similar regulatory ,

to disturb this status quo.

(2021).

licensing, and disciplinary  frameworks. 17  Accord

similar credentialing structure arose in that field.”).
Courts have likewise recognized, since the birth of
modern medical practice, that treatment of the mind,
like treatment of the body, is clinical practice subject
to state oversight. See  Resp’ts’ Br. at 25 (collecting
cases). And states and the federal government require
insurers to treat mental health on equal footing with
other forms of care.18
Petitioner argues that examining the regulation of
“healthcare professions as a whole . . . frame[s] the
historical inquiry at too high a level of generality.”
Pet’r’s Br. at 42. But given the  longstanding clinical
and legal integration of mental health  care within
health care regulation, the regulation of standards of
care in the health  care profession as a whole must
guide the Court’s inquiry.
II. SINCE THE BIRTH OF MODERN MEDICAL
PRACTICE, THE STATE HAS REGULATED
HEALTH CARE PROFESSIONALS’ SPEECH
AS PART OF ITS OVERSIGHT OF CLINICAL
STANDARDS OF CARE
Since the birth of modern medical practice, the

government has reasonably regulated standards of
clinical care. 19  Such regulation has extended to all
kinds of clinical interactions, including those
concerning mental health —many of which involved
nothing but speech.
Indeed, unlike most other areas of communication,
the state’s historical regulation of such standards
extends to the development of medical vocabulary
itself, that enables clinical speech in the first place.
Such regulation enables the maintenance of
standards of clinical care even when such care is
delivered exclusively through speech.
A. Clinical encounters frequently consist
only of speech
Clinical communication between doctor and
patient through counseling, reassurance, and advice,
often with the goal of changing patient behavior, is a
core element of the treatment relationship. Mental
health counselors like Chiles seek to achieve these
goals—but so do primary care providers and
pediatricians. Popular portrayals of medical
professionals and dramatic depictions of emergency
rooms where patients’ lives rely on heroic procedures
by doctors belie the routine practice of medicine,
which primarily  involves conversations between
doctors and patients, to which procedures are often
simply incidental or last resorts.20

19 While Petitioner offers hypothetical legislation regarding clinical care standards, Pet’r’s Br. at 24, any such regulations —like
Colorado’s law at issue here —must still survive rationality review.
20 Tanya Stivers & Alexandra Tate, The Role of Health Care
Communication in Treatment Outcomes , 9 ANN. REV.

Among pediatric patients in particular,
communication forms the lion’s share of care. Well -
child visits are “the most common type of physician
visit for children, and it typically involves guidance
from a physician.” 21  Indeed, Medicaid and CHIP
require coverage of well -child visits, underscoring
that counseling is a core component of pediatric care.22
Well-child treatment and diagnostics often take a
wait-and-see approach when “discerning subtle signs
of emotional or psychological challenges that might
warrant attention.” 23  When intervention is
appropriate, physicians routinely advise patients or
caregivers on injury prevention behaviors such as carseat use, smoke detector maintenance, safe hot water
temperatures, maintenance of stair gates, safe
storage of medication and p oisonous substances, and
supervised access to tubs and pools. 24 Advice tailored
to the specific patient measurably results in improved

B. The government has long regulated medical speech, including advice, as part of
the standard of care
1. Given that speech often constitutes the entirety
of a clinical encounter, states have long applied laws
maintaining standards of care to clinical speech. To be
sure, this Court has explicitly approved much of this
regulation to “facilitate informed consent to a medical
procedure.” NIFLA, 585 U.S. at 770 (citing Casey, 505
U.S. at 899–900 (upholding a law requiring physicians
to obtain informed consent before they could perform
an abortion)); Schloendorff v. Soc’y of N.Y. Hosp., 105
N.E. 92, 93 (N.Y. 1914) (Cardozo, J.); see also
Canterbury v. Spence , 464 F.2d 772, 778 (D.C. Cir.
1972) (evaluating the failure to inform a patient of
risks of operation). Other duties to speak, such as
obtaining a patient’s history or identifying allergies
may also be “tied to a [medical] procedure.” See
NIFLA, 585 U.S. at 770; Stokes v. Dailey, 85 N.W.2d
745, 752 (N.D. 1957); Yorston v. Pennell, 153 A.2d 255,
260 (Pa. 1959).
2. But clinical speech unrelated to any procedure—
as the previous Section describes —goes back more
than 100 years. For example, after dieticians provided
advice during World War I and the Spanish American
War, the first major national association of dietitians
was formed in 1917. 37 During the same era, parents

37 Newman & Surrett, supra note 30, at 1188.

15

sought pediatricians’ advice on issues from
appropriate baby food to disciplinary measures. 38
Indeed, the limits of medical technology during this
era often meant that doctors could primarily offer only
speech-based counsel rather than “procedures” to
effectuate clinical goals. See also Historians’ Br. at 8
(even before the birth of modern practice, “medicine
was primarily performed via speech, i.e., without any
manipulation or touching of the patient”). For
example, while medical professionals were familiar
with germ theory by the turn of the century, it would
be another 50 years before antibiotics were
discovered.39 Doctors therefore could only advise their
patients on various hygiene measures.40 The fact that
mere advice was involved, however, did not allow
doctors to escape liability. “Longstanding torts for
professional malpractice” applied in various
situations where arguably, only speech was involved.
NIFLA, 585 U.S. at 769.
a. Speech cases: Throughout the course of historic
medical practice, incorrect advice, unrelated to any
procedure, had established liability. For example, in
Edwards v. Lamb , 45 A. 480, 480 -81 (N.H. 1899), a
doctor informed a patient’s wife that she could not
become infected from her husband’s wound. The
doctor only made a statement to the wife about her
own risks of infection. Id. Despite the doctor’s
argument that he had not engaged in any conduct per
se, the court held that “[t]he fact that his duty, as to

“inform[ing]” the patient’s wife “that there was no
danger of infection…he voluntarily assumed certain
obligations.” Id. Other cases have similarly held
liability when “advice was given negligently,”
resulting in infection. Skillings v. Allen, 173 N.W. 663,
664 (Minn. 1919).
Such torts were particularly relevant in situations
before antibiotics were discovered, when physicians’
most effective assistance was providing information.41
See id. (collecting cases); Harriott v. Plimpton, 44 N.E.
992, 993 (Mass. 1896) (holding that “the fact that the
purpose of the examination was information, and not
medical treatment is immaterial”). But even today,
doctors can be held liable for incorrect advice —even
when no procedure is involved. See Lininger v.
Eisenbaum, 764 P.2d 1202, 1204 (Colo. 1988) (holding
that a physician's failure to diagnose the hereditary
nature of a child's blindness which led his parents to
conceive a second blind child prov ided a cause of
action); Hofmann v. Blackmon , 241 So. 2d 752, 753
(Fla. Dist. Ct. App. 1970) (recognizing a physician’s
independent duty of accurately communicating
information to a patient, separate from a duty to

Additional duties like informed consent apply even
when a physician’s recommendation is to forgo
medical intervention. Allen v. Harrison, 374 P.3d 812,
817 (Okla. 2016) (discussing that a patient must be

Matthies v. Mastromonaco , 733 A.2d 456, 464 (N.J.
1999) (considering whether a doctor should inform a

b. Diagnosis: In yet another important category of
cases, courts have recognized malpractice liability
even based on a physician’s failure to make and
communicate an accurate diagnosis. See Harris v.
Gallaher, 407 A.2d 531, 532 (Del. 1979) (addressing
negligence when a patient was told not to worry about
a mass in her breast that later proved to be
malignant); Colozzo v. LoVece, 534 N.Y.S.2d 701, 701
(N.Y. App. Div. 1988) (evaluating malpractice when a
pediatrician discharged an infant after assuring
parents of good health, despite the infant having
developed sepsis); Molloy v. Meier , 679 N.W.2d 711,
719 (Minn. 2004) ( holding that physicians acted
negligently by communicating test results as normal
when in reality, the physicians had failed to perform
sufficient genetic tests ). These instances illustrate
how a doctor’s failure to act, and therefore convey
relevant information to the patient, can give rise to
liability.
To be sure, “drawing the line between speech and
conduct can be difficult,” and it might be argued that
the failure to diagnose is inherently tied to the act of
diagnosis itself. NIFLA, 585 U.S. at 769; but see NFIB,
567 U.S. at 555 (recognizing a “difference between
activity and inactivity”). Nonetheless, cases make
clear that even when the task of diagnosis is complete
(and accurate), the failure to communicate that
diagnosis can create liability. See Betesh v. United
States, 400 F. Supp. 238, 246 (D.D.C. 1974) (failing to

18

inform a person of a possible cancer diagnosis creates
liability since an “examinee generally assumes that
‘no news is good news’ and relies on the assumption
that any serious condition will be revealed [when a
doctor conducts a physical examination]”); Oliver v.
Sutton, 540 S.E.2d 645, 648 (Ga. Ct. App. 2000)
(finding that “[a]lthough determining the correct
diagnosis after allegedly misdiagnosing the problem
is certainly not negligence, failing to communicate the
proper diagnosis can be”). Such duties may  also
require a physician to communicate a relevant
diagnosis to a third party. See Pate v. Threlkel , 661
So.2d 278, 282 (Fla. 1995) (concluding that a
physician’s duty runs to certain third parties,
including children, when the children are of a patient
with a genetically transferable nature of a condition).
c. Referral and Gatekeeping: Speech also creates
liability when physicians mishandle referrals or
gatekeeping responsibilities, which are generally
carried out solely through the written or spoken word.
See Scott v. Brookdale Hosp. Ctr. , 400 N.Y.S.2d 552 ,
553 (N.Y. App. Div. 1977) (finding that a failure to
admit a patient, when the patient presents signs of
emergency, is actionable); see also Warren v. Dinter ,
926 N.W.2d 370, 379 (Minn. 2019) (finding that a
hospitalist’s role as a “gatekeeper” for hospita l
admissions can establish a duty of care in professional
negligence even if a physician -patient relationship
does not exist). Similarly, although the patient’s
interactions with a primary care physician and a
specialist may “involve different transactions, entered
into at different times, with different providers,”
NFIB, 567 U.S. at 554, the failure to initiate a referral
to a specialist can still breach the duty of care. Id.; see
King v. Flamm , 442 S.W.2d 679, 681 (Tex. 1969)

(recognizing that “there is a duty to seek consultation
with, and refer the patient to, a specialist”); cf. Larsen
v. Yelle, 246 N.W.2d 841, 844 (Minn. 1976) ( holding
that a general practitioner’s failure to refer a patient
to a specialist does not automatically establish
negligence, but may do so depending on the
circumstances); Davis v. Mercy Med. Ctr., 994 N.W.2d
380, 387 (N.D. 2023) (finding that a physician’s failure
to refer a patient to a nephrologist was the proximate

d. Counseling: Given the regulatory integration of
mental health care into clinical care more generally,
speech-only counseling is routinely regulated under
malpractice standards. See, e.g., Roberts v. Salmi, 866
N.W.2d 460, 474 (Mich. Ct. App. 2014) (recognizing
therapist misconduct if they use inappropriate
treatment techniques); Mower v. Baird, 422 P.3d 837,
844 (Utah 2018) (finding that therapists have a duty
to refrain from recklessly giving rise to false memories
or allegations of sexual abuse); Lovelace v. Urbano, 37
Va. Cir. 114 (Va. Cir. 1995) (upholding a malpractice
verdict against a licensed clinical social worker who
breached the standard of care by failing to intervene
when confronted with information that patient was in
imminent danger of suicide). Psychologists and other
mental health professionals are also subject to
liability for abusive, harassing, or otherwise harmful
speech. See, e.g., Harris v. Kreutzer, 624 S.E.2d 24, 32-
33 (Va. 2006) (holding that a psychologist’s verbally
abusive conduct could support a malpractice claim).
As in other areas of medicine, liability in the mental
health context may arise when care is delivered solely
through speech.

historically overseen clinical practice—some of which

prevents untrained individuals from offering spurious

information. 65  State privacy laws often layer
additional requirements or restrictions.66 HIPAA also
compels disclosures, again, even if no clinical advice is
given, such as providing patients with  a notice of
privacy practice and notifying patients of a breach of

PHI.67
3. To be sure, in some situations, violations of
privacy rules, recordkeeping, and even reporting
requirements have implications for clinical care, and
adherence to these provisions helps ensure that
clinical standards are maintained. See, e.g., DeValk v.
Health Partners, Inc., No. A11-377, 2011 WL 5026346,
at *1-2 (Minn. Ct. App. Oct. 24, 2011) (denying nurse
unemployment because she was fired for misconduct
that included, inter alia, disclosing private health
information and making incorrect claims on pat ient’s
medical records); Catena v. Commonwealth, State Bd.
of Med. Educ. & Licensure , 411 A.2d 869, 870 (Pa.
Commw. Ct. 1980) (considering a violation of
Medicare fraud when physician failed to maintain
records of treatment); Federowicz, 905 S.E.2d at 792
(recognizing a physician’s failure to keep medical
records that reflected patient’s previous attempted
childbirth). But as a whole, these laws serve different
purposes than the historical regulations that define
and enforce the standard of clinical care.
The activity at issue here is the delivery of a
specific counseling treatment that is recognized by
procedure codes (such as CPT 90832 for talk therapy)
and then billed as clinical care. Such treatments fall
squarely within states ’ traditional authority to
regulate the professional practice and is categorically
different from non-clinical speech regimes.

30

III. DISTURBING COLORADO’S REGULATORY
SCHEME WILL PLACE THE COURT IN THE
POSITION OF DECIDING THE CONTENT
OF CLINICAL STANDARDS ACROSS
HEALTH CARE
This Court’s precedents foreclose Petitioner’s
challenge. Colorado’s statute is just one of many state
laws that, whether or not speech is involved, regulate
professional conduct and standards of care. Such
regulation is “subject to reasonable licensing an d
regulation by the State.” Casey, 505 U.S. at 884. This
legal framework, which includes “state regulation[s]
of professional conduct,” NIFLA, 585 U.S. at 769
(quoting NAACP v. Button, 371 U.S. 415, 438 (1963)),
to ensure the safety of its residents and to  maintain
consistent standards and expectations for
practitioners, dates back to the birth of modern
medical practice. Few forms of legal oversight are
more longstanding or “traditional.” Id. Colorado’s
“restriction . . . is part of  [this] long  . . . tradition of
proscription.” Brown v. Ent. Merchs. Ass’n, 564 U.S.
786, 792 (2011). Applying strict First Amendment
scrutiny here would depart from the Court’s doctrinal
framework.
Deference to such regulation is also well advised as
a practical matter. Unlike laws unrelated to
standards of care, such as those mandating reporting
for public safety purposes, laws regulating
professional conduct and standards of care defer to
clinical expertise. Tort law, for exa mple, relies on
expert testimony and licensing boards are made up of
practitioners with expertise in their fields.
Strict scrutiny would render this Court —and the
numerous lower courts in the first instance—arbiters

31

of clinical standards of care, embodied in professional
speech, clinical vocabulary, and ultimately medical
knowledge. That danger is evident from Petitioner’s
and her amici’s own arguments: many focus not
simply on whether counseling is “speech,” but on
whether the clinical content reflects appropriate
science. If courts step into this domain, they will be
drawn into questions they are ill-suited to answer: “Is
the cessation of treatment itself a procedure?” “What
about the refusal to provide treatment?” “ How far
removed must speech be from a procedure before it is
treated differently?” “Who bears responsibility when
counseling and procedures are provided by different
professionals?” These are not constitutional
questions; rather, they are professional heal th care
ones, best answered by clinicians, licensing boards,
and state regulators.
Petitioner ask s this Court to transform the
judiciary into a national medical board. Such a radical
departure would abandon longstanding state
authority, erode patient protections, and destabilize
health care by forcing courts to substitute their
judgment for clinical  consensus. The First
Amendment authorizes no such oversight.
CONCLUSION
This Court should affirm the decision below.
Respectfully submitted.
